citation: Corbett, A. T., & Anderson, J. R. (1995). Knowledge tracing: Modeling the acquisition of procedural knowledge. User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction, 4, 253-278.
supported_claims: Classical BKT represents changing latent skill knowledge with prior, learning, guess, and slip parameters.
The generating assumptions are a deliberately restricted model of procedural skill acquisition, not a complete account of learner behavior.
limits: Programming-tutor setting; does not validate fixed BKT parameters for language learning.
experiment_implication: Retain classical BKT as the clean control, but label its assumptions and vary nuisance mechanisms separately.

citation: Cen, H., Koedinger, K. R., & Junker, B. (2006). Learning Factors Analysis: A general method for cognitive model evaluation and improvement. In ITS 2006, 164-175.
supported_claims: KC models are initially expert hypotheses and can be evaluated and revised through a combination of statistical fit, human expertise, and search.
Predictive improvement alone does not eliminate the need for interpretable expert constraints.
limits: Tutor-log method; discovered factors are not automatically psychological truth.
experiment_implication: Compare declared K* with constrained alternatives while keeping linguistic coherence and pedagogical meaning as gates.

citation: Rupp, A. A., & Templin, J. (2008). The effects of Q-matrix misspecification on parameter estimates and classification accuracy in the DINA model. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 68(1), 78-96.
supported_claims: Deleting required attributes inflated item slip estimates; adding attributes inflated guessing estimates in the studied DINA conditions.
Q misspecification produced high classification errors for affected attribute classes.
limits: Four independent binary attributes under DINA; effect magnitudes do not transfer directly to continuous KT.
experiment_implication: Retain directional omission/addition controls and check whether nuisance effects are absorbed into guess/slip or false KCs.

citation: de la Torre, J., & Chiu, C.-Y. (2016). A general method of empirical Q-matrix validation. Psychometrika, 81(2), 253-273.
supported_claims: Expert-authored Q-matrices remain subjective and should be empirically stress-tested.
A discrimination-index method can flag and replace misspecified entries within G-DINA-family models.
limits: Empirical validation is model-dependent and cannot establish linguistic or pedagogical validity by itself.
experiment_implication: Report structural/empirical Q diagnostics separately from expert linguistic and measurement review.

citation: Gu, Y., & Xu, G. (2021). Sufficient and necessary conditions for the identifiability of the Q-matrix. Statistica Sinica, 31, 449-472.
supported_claims: For strict joint identifiability under DINA, completeness, distinct residual columns, and at least three ones per attribute are jointly necessary and sufficient under the paper's assumptions.
Under general restricted latent class models, at least three items per attribute is necessary for generic joint identifiability; full numerical rank alone is not the theorem's criterion.
limits: Binary latent attributes and specific RLCM assumptions; not a direct theorem for continuous-mastery KT.
experiment_implication: Audit identity/anchor structure, column activation equivalence, and support counts in addition to rank; state which identifiability notion/model is being invoked.

citation: Pardos, Z. A., & Heffernan, N. T. (2011). KT-IDEM: Introducing item difficulty to the knowledge tracing model. In UMAP 2011, 243-254.
supported_claims: Items sharing a skill can differ enough that adding item-specific response parameters can improve KT prediction.
In the reported ASSISTments comparison, mean AUC increased from 0.669 to 0.699; results differed in the Cognitive Tutor setting.
limits: Item-specific guess/slip is one parameterization and can overfit sparse items; predictive gain is not proof of better mastery recovery.
experiment_implication: Make stable item difficulty a planted factor; compare K*, K* plus item effects, and false split-KC models on prediction and oracle recovery.

citation: Khajah, M. M., Huang, Y., Gonzalez-Brenes, J. P., Mozer, M. C., & Brusilovsky, P. (2014). Integrating knowledge tracing and item response theory: A tale of two frameworks. UMAP PALE workshop.
supported_claims: IRT contributes learner-ability and item-difficulty variation while KT contributes temporal learning.
A combined model can represent both sources rather than forcing item and learner variability into skill state.
limits: Workshop evaluation; does not prescribe a universal response function or scale.
experiment_implication: Use crossed learner and item random effects as explicit nuisance variables rather than allowing fine KCs to absorb them.

citation: Yudelson, M. V., Koedinger, K. R., & Gordon, G. J. (2013). Individualized Bayesian Knowledge Tracing Models. In AIED 2013, 171-180.
supported_claims: Student-specific parameters improved prediction for unseen students in the studied tutor datasets.
Individualizing learning speed contributed more than individualizing prior knowledge in that comparison.
limits: Dataset-specific predictive evidence; not a population distribution for human learning rates.
experiment_implication: Include independently planted learner ability and learning-speed heterogeneity, then test whether K* conclusions survive.

citation: Vie, J.-J., & Kashima, H. (2019). Knowledge Tracing Machines: Factorization Machines for Knowledge Tracing. AAAI 2019, 750-757.
supported_claims: A common factorization framework can include learner, item, skill, and temporal features and subsumes several interpretable educational models.
Question identity and side information can materially affect prediction.
limits: Predictive framework; latent interactions need not correspond to pedagogically meaningful KCs.
experiment_implication: Use simple explicit nuisance covariates before interpreting a split KC as a new learnable competence.

citation: Lord, F. M. (1980). Applications of Item Response Theory to Practical Testing Problems. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.
supported_claims: IRT makes item characteristics such as difficulty part of the response model instead of treating same-skill items as exchangeable.
Item calibration, test information, equating, bias, and adaptive testing are distinct measurement concerns.
limits: Assessment framework, not a longitudinal learning model; IRT scales are identified relative to conventions.
experiment_implication: Plant item difficulty on an explicitly standardized scale and never describe chosen numerical values as human constants.

citation: Messick, S. J. (1994). Validity of psychological assessment: Validation of inferences from persons' responses and performances as scientific inquiry into score meaning. ETS Research Report RR-94-45.
supported_claims: Validity concerns inferences and uses, integrating content, substantive, structural, generalizability, external, and consequential evidence.
Construct underrepresentation and construct-irrelevant influences threaten interpretation even when scores are reliable.
limits: General validity theory, not a scoring rubric for platform realism.
experiment_implication: Separate linguistic validity, response-process/answerability evidence, Q structure, and external plausibility instead of using one realism score.

citation: Kane, M. T. (2013). Validating the interpretations and uses of test scores. Journal of Educational Measurement, 50(1), 1-73.
supported_claims: Validation should make the chain of inferences and assumptions from responses to interpretations explicit and evaluate their plausibility.
More ambitious claims require more evidence.
limits: Framework rather than an empirical estimate.
experiment_implication: Write the benchmark's validity argument explicitly: item response -> evidence about K* -> KT inference -> collection recommendation, with rebuttals at each link.

citation: AERA, APA, & NCME (2014). Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing.
supported_claims: Validity evidence can concern test content, response processes, internal structure, relations to other variables, and consequences.
Accessibility and fairness are properties to document, not assumptions.
limits: Standards do not certify any particular synthetic item bank.
experiment_implication: Treat independent learner-solvability probes as response-process stress tests and plan human/expert review for claims they cannot settle.

citation: Rodriguez, M. C. (2003). Construct equivalence of multiple-choice and constructed-response items: A random effects synthesis of correlations. Journal of Educational Measurement, 40(2), 163-184.
supported_claims: Across 29 studies and 56 disattenuated correlations, MC/constructed-response equivalence was heterogeneous.
Using the same stem was associated with correlations approaching unity, whereas non-stem-equivalent designs were less equivalent.
limits: Cross-domain synthesis; correlation does not imply equal difficulty or identical response processes.
experiment_implication: Create genuinely matched stems/cells/Q rows; otherwise content and format effects cannot be separated.

citation: Shohamy, E. (1984). Does the testing method make a difference? The case of reading comprehension. Language Testing, 1(2), 147-170.
supported_claims: Multiple-choice versus open-ended method, text, and response language changed measured difficulty in the study.
Method effects were strongest for lower-level students.
limits: L2 reading comprehension, not grammar production; no direct effect size should be transplanted.
experiment_implication: Cross format with proficiency/ability and inspect interactions, not only an average format intercept.

citation: In'nami, Y., & Koizumi, R. (2009). A meta-analysis of test format effects on reading and listening test performance. Language Testing, 26(2), 219-244.
supported_claims: Across 56 data sources, MC was easier than open-ended formats in L1 reading and L2 listening under the meta-analysis, with heterogeneous effects.
Overall L2-reading effects depended on study-design moderators.
limits: Not a universal MC advantage; domains and designs differ.
experiment_implication: Use zero, moderate, and strong planted format effects and predeclare them as sensitivity scenarios rather than empirical truth.

citation: Purpura, J. E. (2004). Designing test tasks to measure L2 grammatical ability. In Assessing Grammar, 100-145.
supported_claims: Task characteristics can interact with grammatical knowledge, topical knowledge, personal characteristics, and affective schemata to influence performance.
Systematic task design is needed to elicit defensible manifestations of grammatical ability.
limits: Methodological synthesis, not an empirical platform-deployability estimate.
experiment_implication: Represent item format, context, expected response, and scoring rule as first-class measurement metadata.

citation: Kumazawa, T. (2010). The effects of multiple-choice item formats on grammar test performance. JALT Journal, 32(2), 169-.
supported_claims: Six MC grammar formats across 55 items and 608 students differed in difficulty and contribution to score variance.
Even within MC, response format is not an innocuous display choice.
limits: Specific placement/diagnostic context and population.
experiment_implication: Do not collapse all MC or cloze items into a single format label; retain response-mechanism subtypes where tested.

citation: Shavelson, R. J., Baxter, G. P., & Gao, X. (1993). Sampling variability of performance assessments. Journal of Educational Measurement, 30(3), 215-232.
supported_claims: Performance is sampled over tasks, occasions, raters, and methods.
Scores can depend strongly on the task and measurement method sampled.
limits: Performance-assessment studies, not KT sequences.
experiment_implication: Cross each focal KC with multiple lexical contexts and formats; distinguish more learner rows from more measurement facets.

citation: Settles, B., Brust, C., Gustafson, E., Hagiwara, M., & Madnani, N. (2018). Second Language Acquisition Modeling. BEA 2018, 56-65.
supported_claims: The SLAM corpus contains more than seven million produced word tokens from more than 6,000 Duolingo learners across English, Spanish, and French.
The platform traces include multiple response-producing exercise types, timestamps, lesson/practice context, repeated encounters, and token-level error labels.
The sampled cohort selected new users who reached a course-progress threshold, illustrating that platform logs are selected by product and cohort policy.
limits: Vocabulary/morphosyntax is entangled and the cohort is not representative of all platform learners.
experiment_implication: Observable schemas should retain format/session/time and selection-policy metadata; platform-like scheduling must be analyzed as a confound.

citation: Settles, B., & Meeder, B. (2016). A trainable spaced repetition model for language learning. ACL 2016, 1848-1858.
source_type: peer-reviewed conference paper with production data
supported_claims: A production language-learning system used learner-item histories and time gaps to model recall half-lives.
Time and repeated practice are meaningful observable features in language-platform histories.
limits: Primarily lexical recall; half-lives are model estimates, not universal grammar-forgetting constants.
experiment_implication: If forgetting is tested, use elapsed-time/half-life scenarios and explicit timestamps rather than a context-free per-event decay probability.

citation: Geertzen, J., Alexopoulou, T., & Korhonen, A. (2014). Automatic linguistic annotation of large scale L2 databases: The EF-Cambridge Open Language Database (EFCAMDAT). Selected Proceedings of SLRF 2012.
source_type: peer-reviewed corpus paper and official corpus documentation
supported_claims: EFCAMDAT derives from lesson-end writing tasks on an online language school and contains repeated texts with proficiency/course metadata.
Its first release contained 551,036 scripts from 84,864 learners; the official page reports a larger second release.
limits: Extended writing submissions differ from short grammar-practice events; automated annotations carry error.
experiment_implication: Use broad distributions and failure modes from external corpora only as warning checks, not as a target to clone.

citation: Choi, Y., et al. (2020). EdNet: A large-scale hierarchical dataset in education. AIED 2020, 69-73.
supported_claims: EdNet contains 131,441,538 interactions from 784,309 students over more than two years.
Real platform logs include question solving, lecture consumption, purchasing, and within-question actions, not just correctness.
limits: TOEIC-preparation platform; its hierarchy is not transparent grammar-KC truth.
experiment_implication: Keep the benchmark's observable layer minimal but recognize that real histories mix activity types and are shaped by a service policy.

citation: Lindsey, R. V., Shroyer, J. D., Pashler, H., & Mozer, M. C. (2014). Improving students' long-term knowledge retention through personalized review. Psychological Science, 25(3), 639-647.
supported_claims: A semester-long foreign-language study compared time-matched massed, generic spaced, and personalized review schedules.
Personalized review improved the delayed cumulative outcome by 16.5% over massed practice and 10.0% over generic spacing in that setting.
limits: Foreign-language fact/word review in one school context; percentages are not simulator parameters.
experiment_implication: A curriculum/review policy is ecologically plausible, but must be compared with the same opportunity budget and treated as a selection mechanism.

citation: Pavlik, P. I., Jr., & Anderson, J. R. (2008). Using a model to compute the optimal schedule of practice. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 14(2), 101-117.
supported_claims: Practice scheduling trades off spacing, recency, frequency, retrieval success, and time cost.
Uniform repetition is not the only defensible educational schedule.
limits: Memory practice setting; an optimized policy is not necessarily representative of ordinary platform traffic.
experiment_implication: Compare balanced assignment with a simple progressive/review schedule; hold bank and learner world fixed for paired counterfactuals.

citation: Mandel, T., Liu, Y.-E., Levine, S., Brunskill, E., & Popovic, Z. (2014). Offline policy evaluation across representations with applications to educational games. AAMAS 2014, 1077-1084.
supported_claims: Historical educational logs are generated under a behavior policy, making counterfactual policy evaluation a distinct problem.
The paper developed offline evaluation and then tested selected policies with 2,000 real students.
limits: Educational game and policy-value setting; not a direct KT identifiability theorem.
experiment_implication: Record item-selection propensity/policy in synthetic logs and do not treat adaptive observations as random assignments.

citation: Nicholls, D. (2003). The Cambridge Learner Corpus: Error coding and analysis for lexicography and ELT. Corpus Linguistics 2003.
supported_claims: The Cambridge Learner Corpus contained 16 million words from 86 L1 backgrounds at publication, with six million error-coded words.
Its 88-code system distinguishes broad edit operations and linguistic classes, showing that learner errors are structured and multi-level.
limits: Exam essays, proprietary larger corpus, and an annotation taxonomy not aligned one-to-one with K*.
experiment_implication: Derive a small transparent error taxonomy from KC operations, then map it to corpus taxonomies rather than claiming equivalence.

citation: Bryant, C., Felice, M., & Briscoe, T. (2017). Automatic annotation and evaluation of error types for grammatical error correction. ACL 2017, 793-805.
supported_claims: ERRANT aligns learner/corrected sentence pairs and assigns dataset-agnostic edit/error categories at several granularities.
Experts rated at least 95% of automatically extracted edits Good or Acceptable in the reported validation.
limits: Correction-oriented error typing is not failed-KC truth; automatic labels remain imperfect.
experiment_implication: Validate structured errors by the intended edit plus checks for unintended edits; do not infer KCs from ERRANT labels alone.

citation: Bryant, C., Felice, M., Andersen, O. E., & Briscoe, T. (2019). The BEA-2019 Shared Task on Grammatical Error Correction. BEA 2019, 52-75.
supported_claims: W&I+LOCNESS spans learner proficiency bands and retains actual learner writing with corrections.
The test set was corrected five times to better represent alternative valid corrections.
limits: Essay correction differs from constrained learner exercises; multiple references still do not exhaust valid responses.
experiment_implication: For open/cloze production, test multiple plausible answers and preserve accepted-answer provenance instead of exact-string-only scoring.

citation: Wang, Y., & Heffernan, N. T. (2013). Extending knowledge tracing to allow partial credit: Using continuous versus binary nodes. AIED 2013, 181-188.
supported_claims: Binary correctness discards attempt/hint information that can be represented as partial credit.
The reported partial-credit KT variant improved over traditional KT on its real dataset.
limits: Heuristic partial credit and tutoring hints; not evidence that every richer label improves mastery recovery.
experiment_implication: Compare binary correctness with structured error/category information and include shuffled-label controls.

citation: Liu, N., Wang, Z., Baraniuk, R., & Lan, A. (2022). Open-ended Knowledge Tracing for Computer Science Education. EMNLP 2022, 3849-3862.
supported_claims: Exact open-ended responses can carry mastery information hidden by correct/incorrect labels.
Open-response prediction is feasible as a separate KT task in programming education.
limits: Programming submissions and neural response generation; does not validate synthetic language errors.
experiment_implication: Evaluate failed-KC localization and mastery recovery before investing in surface error text.

citation: Kaser, T., & Alexandron, G. (2024). Simulated learners in educational technology: A systematic literature review and a Turing-like test. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 545-585.
supported_claims: Simulated-learner studies commonly model narrow aspects of learning.
The review found that nearly half of included studies offered no evidence addressing simulator validity.
limits: A Turing-like test is one proposed criterion and behavioral indistinguishability is not sufficient for causal validity.
experiment_implication: Validate each simulator world against its purpose using distributional diagnostics, held-out qualitative traces, and adversarial critics; never call complexity realism by default.

citation: Rosenberg-Kima, R. B., & Pardos, Z. A. (2014). Is this data for real? BKT20y Workshop / EDM 2014 Extended Proceedings.
supported_claims: Two six-item ASSISTments datasets fitted BKT values (prior, learn, guess, slip) of (.453, .068, .270, .156) and (.701, .044, .243, .165).
Similar BKT likelihood surfaces did not by themselves establish that simulated data reproduced all real mechanisms.
limits: Only two short, fixed-order skill datasets and fitted model parameters; values are not human-language constants.
experiment_implication: A bounded sensitivity grid such as learn 0.02/0.05/0.10 and guess/slip spanning roughly 0.05-0.25 is defensible as a scenario grid, explicitly not an estimate of people.

citation: Klingler, S., Kaser, T., Solenthaler, B., & Gross, M. (2015). On the performance characteristics of latent-factor and knowledge tracing models. EDM 2015, 37-44.
supported_claims: Synthetic truth permits systematic testing across tens of thousands of parameter configurations and controlled violations.
Different KT/latent-factor models have different best- and worst-case regions.
limits: Synthetic model family determines the tested worlds; coverage is not ecological validation.
experiment_implication: Prefer separate clean, difficulty, format, heterogeneity, error, and schedule worlds over one opaque realism simulator.

citation: Caines, A., Yannakoudakis, H., Allen, H., Perez-Paredes, P., Byrne, B., & Buttery, P. (2022). The Teacher-Student Chatroom Corpus version 2: More lessons, new annotation, automatic detection of sequence shifts. NLP4CALL 2022, 23-35.
supported_claims: TSCC v2 contains 260 one-to-one English lessons, about 41.4K turns and 363K tokens across its two releases.
Its annotation distinguishes sequence shifts and functions including exercise, free practice, eliciting, scaffolding, repair, clarification, revision, grammar, lexis, and meaning.
limits: Small number of teachers/learners and human tutoring; annotations do not define atomic KT opportunities.
experiment_implication: Pilot dialogue as a continuum and annotate opportunity boundaries explicitly; quantify ambiguity and incidental targets rather than treating every turn as one item.

citation: Dzikovska, M. O., Moore, J. D., Steinhauser, N., & Campbell, G. (2010). The impact of interpretation problems on tutorial dialogue. ACL 2010 Short Papers, 43-48.
supported_claims: Unrestricted input supports contentful talk but creates unavoidable interpretation failures.
Non-standard terminology and non-understanding affected user satisfaction and learning in the evaluated tutorial dialogue system.
limits: Electronics tutor, not L2 grammar; system interpretation errors are only one source of ambiguity.
experiment_implication: Treat dialogue/open production as introducing measurement noise and recovery events; compare determinacy and error attribution with constrained formats.

citation: Dzikovska, M., Isard, A., Bell, P., Moore, J., Steinhauser, N., & Campbell, G. (2011). BEETLE II: An adaptable tutorial dialogue system. SIGDIAL 2011, 338-340.
supported_claims: A deployable tutorial dialogue interaction includes curriculum material, task context, dialogue history, student explanations, feedback policy, and recovery behavior.
Different dialogue policies change the interaction corpus.
limits: Short system description and non-language domain.
experiment_implication: A dialogue item cannot be represented faithfully by prompt text alone; store visible context, turn state, expected response function, and feedback assumptions.
